projects.name: Candlestick Point
projects.acresNote: OCII describes the approximately 272-acre Candlestick Point area; the 2024 CEQA notice of determination gives 271.6 acres. It includes the former stadium and parking lots, the Alice Griffith housing site and the Candlestick Point State Recreation Area. Older Planning documents (2013–2018) said roughly 281 acres.

program.notes: 2024 Modified Project Variant (OCII, Sept 2024). R&D/office rose from 750,000 to 2,800,000 sq ft after about 2,050,000 sq ft moved from Hunters Point Shipyard Phase 2. Retail is 170,000 sq ft regional plus 134,500 sq ft neighborhood. About 34% of Candlestick's 7,218 homes will be below market rate (OCII), counting workforce homes for households earning 120–160% of AMI; across Candlestick Point and Shipyard Phase 2 together the share is about 32% (3,363 of 10,672). The first phase covers seven city blocks with about 700 homes, 314 of them affordable. The Mayor's office cites 100 acres of parks and open space; OCII's open-space count (105.7 acres) includes the existing State Recreation Area.

projects.developer: FivePoint Holdings, LLC (previously Lennar Urban)
publicPartners: SF Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure (OCII)
projects.stageNote: The Mayor broke ground on Sept 9, 2026 on the first new phase: seven city blocks (four mixed-use residential blocks on Harney Way, two residential blocks on Arelious Walker Drive and a commercial parcel in Candlestick Center) with about 700 homes, 314 of them affordable. Roads and utilities come first (OCII: 2026–2028, then housing and commercial buildings); no building permits have been issued for the blocks yet. The 2024 amendments split the Candlestick build-out into seven major phases instead of three.

It was planned together with Hunters Point Shipyard until 2024, when the city found the two could no longer be built in concert and let Candlestick go ahead on its own.

projects.name: Hunters Point Shipyard
projects.acresNote: Shipyard Phase 2: 421.0 acres per the 2024 CEQA notice of determination and OCII. Phase 2 is all of the shipyard except the Hilltop and Hillside (Phase 1); 2018 Planning Commission items said roughly 402 acres. The whole shipyard peninsula is about 490 acres.

Proposition F (2014) allows 1–2 million sq ft of commercial and office space; the EIR studied up to about 2.26 million gsf of office. Buildings 2, 12 and 21 are kept and rehabilitated. projects.name: Mission Bay
projects.acresNote: OCII: the Mission Bay North (65 acres) and Mission Bay South (238 acres) redevelopment project areas cover 303 acres between San Francisco Bay and Interstate 280.

program.notes: OCII figures: 2,964 homes (698 affordable) and 6.5 acres of parks in Mission Bay North; 3,571 homes (1,218 affordable) and 34 acres of parks in Mission Bay South. Mission Bay South has 6.1 million sq ft of commercial and institutional space and 429 hotel rooms; Mission Bay North about 200,000 sq ft of commercial space. Includes UCSF's research campus and the Warriors' event center on an approximately 11-acre site. Ordinance 22-26 (Feb 2026) raised Mission Bay South's planned homes from about 3,440 to 3,690, adding 250 affordable homes on Block 4 East. Mission Bay North has no hotel; the 429 hotel rooms are in Mission Bay South.

projects.developer: FOCIL-MB LLC (successor to the original master developer, Catellus Development Corporation)
publicPartners: SF Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure (OCII)
projects.stageNote: Largely built. Block 12 West, the last residential site, has no housing entitlement left; OCII and FOCIL propose about 535 homes there, with approvals expected in early 2027. The city's 2026 capital plan expects nine more Mission Bay parks over the next four years.

projects.acresNote: A rail line, not a site: a 1.3-mile tunnel from Fourth and King to the Salesforce Transit Center, 2.2 miles of total construction including trackwork in Caltrain's Fourth and King railyard (TJPA, 2026). No official footprint acreage was found. The 2018 Final SEIS/EIR gave longer lengths (2.7 miles with a turnback track at Mariposa Street, 2 miles without it), which have since been superseded. program.notes: A transit project, so the building program fields do not apply. Scope: a mostly underground rail extension along Townsend and Second Streets, built by cut-and-cover and mined tunneling. It includes a new underground Fourth and Townsend Street Station (two tracks, a center platform and two side platforms, serving Caltrain), the fit-out of the existing two-level train box under the Salesforce Transit Center (six tracks and three center platforms for Caltrain and high-speed rail), ventilation and emergency exit structures, and trackwork in Caltrain's Fourth and King railyard. The 2026 scope changes removed the high-speed rail platforms at Fourth and Townsend, the train box extension and the intercity bus facility. They also shortened the tunnel stub box by about 750 feet. Project budget: $8.255 billion in year-of-expenditure dollars (2023 estimate, including the completed train box, contingency and financing). The 2025 updated estimate is about $7.572 billion, and TJPA holds the difference as unallocated contingency. FTA's Capital Investment Grant share is $3.38 billion. TJPA's July 2026 funding plan lists $1,304 million committed from non-CIG sources, $1,303 million in planned state funds, $265 million in other planned sources and $729 million already invested in the train box, which leaves a $587 million gap. TJPA forecasts over 125,000 average daily riders.

program.notes: A transit project, so the building program fields do not apply. The approved project (Alternative A) runs high-speed trains on Caltrain's electrified tracks rather than a new dedicated line. It would modify about 17.4 miles of existing track, mostly within the Caltrain right-of-way, add no passing tracks, build a light maintenance facility in East Brisbane and modify eight existing stations or platforms. It would also add safety upgrades at 40 at-grade crossings, 8.8 miles of new fencing and 21 radio towers. High-speed rail stations: Fourth and King in San Francisco (interim, until The Portal brings trains to the Salesforce Transit Center), Millbrae (for SFO and BART) and San Jose Diridon. Gilroy, the next station south, is in the San Jose to Merced section. The Final EIR/EIS (June 2022) estimated the preferred alternative at about $5,317 million in 2021 dollars. The 2026 Business Plan estimates the 'San Francisco to Gilroy Blended Approach' at $1,273 million (year-of-expenditure dollars, San Francisco–Bakersfield scenario; $1,291 million in the Phase 1 scenario). That figure excludes the San Jose to Gilroy upgrades ($2 to $5 billion, a 'shared benefit' project) and The Portal. The Authority contributed $714 million to Caltrain's electrification of the 51 miles between San Francisco and San José, which high-speed trains will share.

projects.name: BART station-area housing

projects.acresNote: Sum of the acreages BART's TOD Work Plan GIS layer gives for the parcels drawn at the six sites: West Oakland 5.5, Lake Merritt 2.8, North Berkeley 8.1, Ashby West Lot 4.5, El Cerrito Plaza 7.5 and Amador Station 3.6. At North Berkeley, Ashby and El Cerrito Plaza the parcels include station entrances and track land that won't be built on (El Cerrito's approved master plan site is about 6 acres plus the 0.48-acre Parcel A South).

program.notes: Homes are a sum of the official per-site figures: West Oakland 762 (522 market rate, 240 affordable), Lake Merritt 557, North Berkeley 739, Ashby West Lot up to 600, El Cerrito Plaza 743 and Amador Station 300 in two buildings of 136 and 164 (3,701, with Ashby at its upper figure). Office is a sum too: about 300,000 sq ft at West Oakland and up to 500,000 sq ft at Lake Merritt. Affordable homes by site: 240 at West Oakland, 233 at Lake Merritt, 381 at North Berkeley, half of Ashby's, 350 at El Cerrito Plaza and all 300 at Amador Station. Retail: about 53,000 sq ft at West Oakland, up to 16,500 sq ft at Lake Merritt and smaller ground-floor spaces elsewhere. Walnut Creek's last phase (about 240 homes, in planning) isn't counted.

projects.developer: Six teams selected by BART: Mandela Station Partners and Mandela Station Affordable (West Oakland); Strada Investment Group and East Bay Asian Local Development Corporation (Lake Merritt); North Berkeley Housing Partners (BRIDGE Housing, EBALDC, Insight Housing and AvalonBay Communities); Adeline Alliance Partners with Resources for Community Development (Ashby); Holliday Development, Related California and Satellite Affordable Housing Associates (El Cerrito Plaza); and The Related Companies of California (Amador Station)
projects.stageNote: Three sites are under construction: El Cerrito Plaza's first building (since November 2025), Lake Merritt's senior building (since October 2024; BART expects completion in spring 2027) and West Oakland's 240 affordable homes (since September 2026). North Berkeley is entitled (December 2024) and Amador Station, approved in 2021, is waiting for funding, and the City of Dublin is reviewing building permits for its first building. The Ashby West Lot has a developer (negotiating agreement signed February 2026) but no application with the City yet.

projects.summary: BART is building housing on its station parking lots. This entry maps the six sites where that work isn't finished: West Oakland, Lake Merritt, North Berkeley, Ashby, El Cerrito Plaza and Amador Station in Dublin. Together they plan about 3,700 homes, about half of them affordable, plus up to 800,000 sq ft of offices in Oakland. BART says the program has already delivered 4,232 homes and 874,000 sq ft of commercial space at 15 stations.
